evidence.text: A wreck preserves a group of associated objects; it provides a shipment context but not a complete itinerary.

production.text: Hull construction, anchors and cargo connect seafaring skill with the movement of raw materials and finished goods.

coordination.text: Cargo, anchors, joints and tools connect different stages of production and transport. Ownership, crew identity and every stop remain interpretive questions.

name: Uluburun: a cargo beneath the sea
place: Off Kaş, eastern Mediterranean coast of Türkiye
geographicPrecision: Wreck-region locator in southwestern Anatolia; no exact ship track is reconstructed.

interval.label: c. 1320 BCE ±15 years
interval.note: Dating reported by the excavators’ project page; not an exact sailing or sinking year.

question: What traveled together on one ship?
summary: The Uluburun wreck preserves a shipment and traces of the people and skills that kept a ship working. Copper, tin, containers and valuable goods occurred together near the Anatolian coast. That association is secure evidence of movement, but recovering objects is different from identifying their ore sources, owners or destinations. The findspot, cargo and proposed origins need different visual and verbal labels.

sections.title: One archaeological association, several kinds of work
sections.text: INA’s account identifies copper and tin ingots alongside pottery, foodstuffs and luxury materials. Raw metal could move toward later manufacture while finished objects travelled for other uses. A shipment thus joins production, packing, transport and exchange rather than representing one self-contained craft. The excavators’ date, c. 1320 BCE ±15 years, remains an approximate wreck window. Neither that window nor a mixed cargo identifies every port visited, the intended buyer or the political arrangement behind the voyage.

citations.locator: Date header; cargo and economic exchange

sections.title: The hull was equipment, not just a container
sections.text: Cedar planking, pegged mortise-and-tenon joints and anchors reveal material arrangements that made maritime transport possible. Pulak’s 1990 report records exposed hull members, tools and objects interpreted cautiously as possible raw material or spare parts. Such details bring building and maintenance into view beside the prestige goods. They do not provide a complete workday or a roster of specialists. Personal effects can support proposals about people aboard, but a vessel style or weapon should not become a certain nationality or a named passenger.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 9–10; Fig. 2 and possible spare material

sections.title: The seabed is not an untouched loading plan
sections.text: Excavators worked through sediment and encrustation across a steep site. The campaign report describes objects rolling or falling downslope and distinguishes exposed hull structure from loose material. The association still matters, but the position in which an object was recovered is not automatically its original stowage position. A useful reconstruction must explain preservation and movement as well as cargo categories. The teaching diagram therefore groups evidential questions; it does not draw invented stacks in a reconstructed hold.

citations.locator: Printed p. 9, catchment and slope movement; pp. 10–11

sections.title: A chemical match is an argument about origin
sections.text: A 2022 study linked tin samples with Central Asian and Anatolian sources. A 2023 critique challenged those assignments and offered alternatives. Work published in 2025 adds evidence concerning contamination and remelting, complicating the interpretation of the Uluburun material. These analyses make the history richer without providing a universally agreed ore-source map. The diagram marks origins as inferred and contested. It leaves the ship’s complete itinerary unresolved and keeps the securely located wreck separate from proposed paths to it.

returnPrompt: Choose one object category: what is secure about its association, what is inferred about its origin, and what remains unknown about its movement?

deeperReading.title: Do not turn every cargo into a royal gift
deeperReading.text: The project page frames the shipment in relation to elite exchange and wealthy audiences. Pulak’s earlier report describes a possible royal connection rather than an identified owner. Balance weights, varied goods, tools and hull remains can support questions about trade and shipboard practice without proving one model of ownership for every object. Palace demand and merchants’ work need not be treated as mutually exclusive explanations before the evidence is examined. A future account should investigate the financing and stages of exchange with precisely dated texts rather than supplying an invented manifest or a universal Bronze Age market.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 8–10, tentative royal attribution and weights

deeperReading.title: Recycling can complicate a geological fingerprint
deeperReading.text: Comparing an ingot with an ore depends on what happened between extraction and recovery. Contamination, mixing and recasting can alter the signals being compared. Williams and colleagues discuss these problems specifically for Uluburun; their stronger source arguments for other Mediterranean wrecks cannot simply be copied onto this cargo. Keep the 2022 analysis and later challenges together when evaluating a claim. No exact Central Asian, Anatolian or British share is presented here as settled, and even a well-supported source region would not establish every intermediary or the route taken by the ship.

familyActivity.title: Sort found, inferred and unknown
steps: Find the wreck location and recovered materials in the solid part of the diagram. Name two things found together.
Find the dashed origin panel. Explain what extra work is needed to argue where a metal came from.
Name one question the wreck does not settle, such as the full itinerary or the owner of every object.
familyActivity.explanation: The diagram groups types of evidence. It is not a map of a confirmed sailing route, a stowage plan or a passenger list.

evidenceReading.title: Read a shipment through changing investigations
evidenceReading.introduction: Paraphrases distinguish a field report, a later project summary and competing laboratory interpretations.

items.label: A campaign report is an interim record
items.text: The 1990 report describes excavated material and interpretation during an unfinished excavation, including objects displaced downslope.
items.interpretation: Its observations help explain recovery. Interim cargo totals and provisional identifications should not be relabelled as the final excavation inventory.

items.label: Source assignments are contested
items.text: Powell and colleagues proposed specific tin-source regions in 2022; Berger and colleagues challenged key assignments in 2023.
items.interpretation: A laboratory dataset and the historical geography argued from it are different levels of claim. A disputed source allocation is not a confirmed shipping route.

items.label: A newer paper does not make all wrecks identical
items.text: The 2025 study discusses variable lead contamination and possible remelting in Uluburun ingots while making source arguments for other wrecks.
items.interpretation: Read the Uluburun-specific qualification on p. 718. Do not transfer another assemblage’s stronger attribution to this ship.

review.scope: Bounded C2 account with main/deeper/evidence reading, separate reference chronology, family entry and source-labelled visuals.
limitations: No licensed historical wreck photograph was added; the new image is a modern evidence diagram.
Crew, ownership, destination and tin provenance remain qualified. The 2022 paper’s figures and supplements were not visually inspected.
The 1990 issue and specified 2025 paper pages were read, not every publication in the excavation bibliography.
